analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and health insurers to publish their actual negotiated prices, with fines for hiding them.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill introduced by the House committee's chair and its top Democrat never received a committee vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Transparent PRICE Act would write hospital price disclosure into law, requiring hospitals to post what they actually charge — list prices, cash prices, and the rates negotiated with each insurer — in a standard government format, with fines starting at $10 per bed per day and a $5 million minimum for large hospitals that stay out of compliance for a year. It would also require health insurers to publish their negotiated rates and drug payment data every three months, and to offer patients a real-time tool showing what a service will cost them out of pocket before they get it. The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and employers. Before getting care, patients could see what a hospital charges an insurer, what it charges cash customers, and what their own out-of-pocket cost would be. Employers buying coverage for workers could compare plans' actual negotiated rates instead of negotiating blind. Uninsured and cash-paying patients would see the discounted cash price they are entitled to. Consumers would also get a public list naming hospitals that refuse to comply.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must post, in a consumer-friendly machine-readable format, the gross charge, discounted cash price, and payer-specific negotiated charges for at least 300 shoppable services, described in plain language with billing codes [S2][S3].

Hospitals that fail to comply after notice and a 90-day corrective window face civil fines of $10 per bed per day (up to $300 per day for hospitals with 30 beds or fewer), and hospitals with more than 30 beds that stay out of compliance for a full year face a fine of at least $5 million — far stiffer than the existing rule's enforcement [S3].

The Health and Human Services Secretary must maintain a public, real-time list of hospitals out of compliance — including who got warnings, corrective action requests, or fines — and a list of hospitals in compliance, and must report enforcement activity to Congress each year [S2][S3].

Health plans must submit their in-network negotiated rates, out-of-network payment amounts, and net-of-rebate drug payment data every three months in comparable machine-readable files that anyone can access free and without an account [S3].

Plans must offer a self-service tool that tells a patient in real time the in-network rate, their cost sharing, how much deductible they have already met, and any prior authorization or step-therapy requirements that apply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers. They bear the cost of building the data systems, posting granular rate data every quarter, and facing fines. The bigger cost is competitive: once negotiated rates are public, hospitals with higher prices and insurers with worse deals can be compared directly, pressuring their pricing. Pharmacy benefit managers' rebate-driven drug pricing would also be exposed, since plans must report what they actually pay for drugs net of rebates.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is a real burden: hospitals and insurers must publish rates for thousands of items and services in machine-readable formats and update them quarterly, a cost that falls hardest on smaller hospitals [S3].

Publicly posting payer-specific negotiated rates could disrupt price negotiation itself — providers who quietly give better deals may face pressure to raise those rates, and negotiated discounting may shrink, so the net effect on prices is uncertain.

Transparency alone does not guarantee lower bills: patients only benefit if they can act on prices in advance, and the bill relies on enforcement by the Secretary and annual GAO review rather than guaranteeing price reductions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the potential upside is large and the downside modest — knowing prices before care is genuinely useful and the fines finally give the existing transparency rules teeth. The main honest caveats are the compliance burden on smaller hospitals and the possibility that exposing negotiated discounts changes how rates get negotiated. The bill's fatal weakness was not its design but that it never moved: with the strongest possible committee backing, it still got no vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee from the day it was introduced until the 118th Congress ended — its sponsor chaired that committee and its only cosponsor was the committee's top Democrat, but no markup or floor vote was ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA), chair of the Energy and Commerce Committee, introduced the bill on April 18, 2023 together with Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ), the committee's ranking Democrat [S1][S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without ever receiving a committee markup or a floor vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health insurers kept the status quo: no statutory requirement to publish negotiated rates, no public compliance lists, and the penalty minimums in the existing rules remained in place rather than rising to $5 million. Patients and employers continued negotiating without seeing prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers kept opaque pricing

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan leadership support — a Republican committee chair and the committee's ranking Democrat — and no recorded opposition, yet it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists to break down support by party.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to post their chargemaster prices, discounted cash prices, and per-insurer negotiated rates in a standard format, with a public noncompliance list and fines reaching a $5 million minimum for large hospitals that stay out of compliance for a year. Because hospitals currently earn more where prices are opaque, exposure of negotiated rates runs directly against their financial interest and alongside patients' interest in knowing prices in advance.

Insurers would have to publish all in-network negotiated rates and out-of-network payments every three months in comparable public files, and build real-time cost-sharing tools showing patients their actual out-of-pocket cost. Public rate files let employers and patients compare insurers' deals, which pressures the negotiated rates that shape insurer-provider bargaining.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and rebate intermediaries
industries.note: Plans would have to report what they actually pay for each drug net of rebates, discounts, and price concessions. Because rebate-driven intermediaries profit from the spread between list prices and net prices, mandatory net-price disclosure runs against their interest.
Employers buying health coverage could see the rates their plans pay every provider, giving them real data for the first time to negotiate lower costs for the coverage they provide workers.
